html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Carry out or check an impact assessment of the chosen system
  • Identify and weigh the key terms and risks of a vendor or license agreement
  • See what running your own proprietary model gains and costs
  • Know when a deployer becomes a provider, and what follows

2IV.B.1: Assess the impact of the system that was chosen, or review that assessment

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Perform, so the depth is Apply. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Running case

The Chosen Assistant, the Contract and an In-House Idea

  • Samira Haddad asks for an impact assessment on the chosen assistant, not the design-stage one
  • Ravi Menon and Jonas Weber review the Corvid Labs agreement: data use, indemnity and notice of model changes
  • A proposal appears to build an in-house model; Samira Haddad asks what that would change
  • Your task: assess the system, weigh the contract, and compare building with buying

Assessing the System You Chose: What Is Different Now

  • In module 8 you assessed a planned use case; now you assess the system that was actually selected
  • It is your use, your people and your data, which the provider's assessment cannot cover
  • Evidence comes from the provider's documents and your own tests and pilots
  • The result feeds a go, go with conditions or no-go decision, with owners and monitoring triggers
  • It is reviewed again when the system, the use or the law changes

Exam tip: The provider assesses the product; the deployer assesses the use.

Gathering the Evidence: Provider Documents and Your Own Tests

  • Instructions for use (Article 13): intended purpose, limits, oversight measures, logs
  • Model or system card: performance by group and evaluation conditions
  • Test, audit and certification reports, and any provider risk assessment
  • Your own pilot and test results on your data and your users
  • Gaps are findings: missing documents, vague claims and untested conditions go on the risk list
  • Ask the provider in writing: no answer is an answer

Exam tip: Treat provider documents as claims to check against your own tests, not as proof.

Deployer Duties That Feed the Assessment

  • Article 26: use the system as the instructions say, give human oversight to people with competence, training and authority, and check that input data are relevant and representative
  • Monitor the system, inform the provider, suspend use if there is a risk, and report any serious incident
  • Keep logs for at least six months, and tell workers and affected people about the use
  • Article 27: public bodies, providers of public services and deployers of certain credit and insurance systems assess fundamental rights impact before first use, and may cross-refer to a DPIA (Article 35)
  • The assessment sets up these duties: oversight roles, data checks, monitoring and notices
  • Helios: its policy requires an assessment of every system, whatever the law requires

Exam tip: Article 26 applies to every deployer of a high-risk system; Article 27 reaches only certain deployers.

Reviewing an Existing Assessment

  • A review asks whether an existing assessment (the provider's, a predecessor's or an earlier version) still fits
  • Is it current and in scope for your use, people and setting?
  • Is it backed by evidence, and does it cover affected groups, including vulnerable people?
  • Do mitigations have owners and dates, and are reassessment triggers named?
  • Reuse what holds, fill the gaps, and record what changed
  • Triggers: new version, new use, new data, an incident or a new law

Exam tip: A reused assessment is acceptable only if it matches your use; otherwise update it.

Helios: The Impact Assessment on the Chosen Assistant

  • Scope: the Corvid Labs model, used through an interface, grounded on Helios's support documents and answering customers in public chat
  • Findings: wrong or outdated answers can harm customers and trust; chats may hold personal data; some customers may be vulnerable or rely on an answer
  • Evidence: the provider's documents, a pilot on real questions and Helios's own test results
  • Conditions for go: owners and review dates for the support documents; the assistant says when it does not know and offers a person; a monitoring and incident plan; trained support staff
  • Decision: go with conditions, reviewed when the model version, the documents or the use change

Exam tip: The output of an impact assessment is a decision with conditions, not a score.

3IV.B.2: Find and weigh the key terms and risks in a vendor or license agreement

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Identify, so the depth is Understand. The course has 3 practice questions on this indicator.

Why the Contract Is a Governance Control

  • A vendor or license agreement is where the provider's promises and limits are written down
  • It allocates risk between provider and customer, and is evidence for audits and regulators
  • It is also the customer's best leverage: terms are hardest to change after signing
  • Six families of terms: data, intellectual property, security, performance and audit, liability, change and exit
  • Review with procurement, legal and privacy, security and the business owner
  • Helios: Ravi Menon and Jonas Weber lead the Corvid Labs review

Exam tip: Governance tools are not only policies: the contract is one.

Data Terms: Use, Ownership, Retention and Location

  • Use of your data: may the provider use your prompts and files to train or improve its models? Prefer no, unless you agree
  • Ownership: who owns inputs and outputs, and any fine-tuned version?
  • Processor terms: for personal data, GDPR Article 28(3) requires a binding contract: documented instructions, confidentiality, security, sub-processor conditions, help with data subject requests, deletion or return, and audit information
  • Sub-processors: Article 28(4): bound by the same obligations, and the first processor stays fully liable
  • Retention and location: how long data are kept, how they are deleted, and where they are processed (Articles 44 to 49)

Exam tip: The first data question for any generative AI vendor is whether your inputs train its model.

Intellectual Property: Ownership, Training Data and Indemnity

  • Outputs: who owns or may use what the system produces, and are there restrictions on use?
  • Training data: does the provider warrant its rights to the training data? (module 5)
  • Indemnity: will the provider defend and compensate the customer if the model or its output is said to infringe someone's rights, and what exclusions apply, such as misuse or edited output?
  • General-purpose model providers need a copyright policy and must publish a training-content summary (Article 53(1)): ask for both
  • Your inputs: your own IP and confidential content must not be reused without permission

Exam tip: Indemnity clauses come with conditions and exclusions: read what they leave out.

Security and Confidentiality Terms Beyond the BoK

  • Security commitments: access controls, encryption, testing, recognized certifications and a right to see the evidence
  • Confidentiality: your prompts, files and outputs stay confidential, with limits on staff and sub-processor access
  • Incident notice: a fixed, short time to tell you; a processor must notify the controller without undue delay (GDPR Article 33(2)), and your own reporting clocks (module 10) can be short
  • AI-specific security: protection against prompt injection, data leakage and model theft, and a way to handle vulnerabilities
  • Sub-processors and location: named, notified and bound by the same terms (module 4)

Exam tip: Your own reporting clocks can be short, so the contract must say how fast the vendor must tell you.

Performance, Documentation and Audit Rights

  • Service levels: availability, response and support times, with remedies if missed
  • Performance statements: accuracy and limits, ideally by group, and what follows if they are not met
  • Documentation: instructions for use and model information (Article 13), kept current
  • Testing and audit rights: to test, assess or audit the system, or receive independent reports; a processor must support audits (Article 28(3))
  • Cooperation: where a high-risk system is built on a supplier's parts, a written agreement on information, capabilities and technical access (Article 25(4))

Exam tip: Without documentation and audit rights, a customer cannot do its own oversight and assessment.

Liability, Indemnities and Insurance Beyond the BoK

  • Liability caps: often limited to the fees paid; check whether data breach, IP and confidentiality are carved out or have a higher cap
  • Exclusions: vendors may exclude losses from errors in AI output; know what stays with you
  • Indemnities: defense and payment for named claims, such as IP or data breach caused by the vendor
  • Contracts allocate loss between the parties; they do not remove duties to regulators or to affected people
  • Insurance: ask about the vendor's cover, and check your own policy for AI-related losses
  • Helios: Jonas Weber asks for a higher cap for data and IP claims

Exam tip: A liability cap limits what the vendor pays you, not what you owe to others.

Change, Notice and Exit Beyond the BoK

  • Model changes: the provider may update or replace the model, so require advance notice of material changes, release notes and time to retest; consider version pinning
  • Deprecation: how long an old version stays available
  • Subcontractors and changed terms: notice and a right to object or leave
  • Exit: termination rights, return and deletion of data, transition help and continued access to logs
  • Lock-in: formats, portability and alternatives
  • Helios: an unannounced model change could invalidate the tests and the impact assessment (module 10)

Exam tip: Unannounced model changes break test results, so write notice and retest time into the contract.

Weighing the Terms: Red Flags and a Review Checklist Beyond the BoK

  • Read the agreement for what each term allocates and what is missing
  • Red flags: training on your data, no indemnity, caps with no carve-outs, silent model changes, no audit rights, no incident notice
  • Weigh the terms against the risk of the use: a hiring tool needs more than a spelling helper
  • Negotiate what matters, and record accepted gaps with compensating controls
  • Escalate unresolved high risks to the committee (module 2)

Exam tip: Match the strictness of the terms to the risk of the use, and record any gap you accept.

4IV.B.3: Understand the risks and opportunities of deploying your own proprietary model

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Identify, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Deploying Your Own Model: What Changes

  • A proprietary model of your own is one the company develops, or has developed, and runs under its own name
  • A provider develops an AI system or model and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name (Article 3(3))
  • Helios today: a deployer of the hiring tool, and of the model behind the assistant (module 6)
  • In-house build: Helios would also become the provider, with the developer's duties from modules 8 to 10
  • No vendor stands between you and the user: documentation, testing and monitoring become yours
  • Putting your name on a high-risk system, or substantially modifying one, also makes you the provider (Article 25(1))

Exam tip: Building your own model moves you from the deployer's side to the provider's.

More Obligations: The Provider's Duties

  • If the system is high-risk, the provider meets the requirements in Articles 9 to 15: risk management, data governance, documentation, logs, instructions, oversight, accuracy and security
  • Article 16: a quality management system (Article 17), documentation and logs
  • Before release: conformity assessment (Article 43), declaration (Article 47), CE marking (Article 48), registration (Article 49)
  • After release: post-market monitoring (Article 72) and serious incident reporting (Article 73)
  • General-purpose model: the Article 53(1) duties (module 6)
  • As the user of its own system, the company keeps the deployer duties too

Exam tip: Own model, own duties: everything the provider owes in modules 8 to 10 now falls on you.

Higher Potential Liability [Dates]

  • No vendor to share the blame: claims about defects, bias or harm come to you as the maker
  • Product liability: the new EU Product Liability Directive covers software and AI systems and applies to products placed on the market from 9 December 2026
  • Makers can be liable for defects that appear through updates or machine learning (module 5)
  • Regulatory exposure: the provider-level duties and fines of the AI Act (module 6)
  • Contract exposure: your customers' contracts may promise more than you can deliver
  • Reduce it: strong documentation, testing evidence, monitoring, incident handling, insurance and clear terms of use
  • As of 27 October 2026: check how the Directive applies to your product before release

Exam tip: Building your own system makes you the party that injured people and authorities turn to.

Opportunities: Control, Fit and Advantage

  • Opportunities: control over data, behavior and update timing; better fit to your domain; ownership of the resulting IP; less dependence on a vendor; possible lower cost at scale; differentiation
  • Costs and duties: the provider's obligations, higher liability, specialist talent and infrastructure, ongoing retraining and monitoring, and security of weights and data
  • Honest accounting: weigh the opportunities against the obligations, not the first alone
  • Helios: an in-house assistant could keep data inside the company, but Helios would need new skills and a quality management system

Exam tip: Control comes with accountability: the opportunities and the obligations arrive together.

Build, Buy or Both: Deciding With Eyes Open

  • Buy: the fastest start; the provider carries the build duties; the contract is your main control
  • Open model you host: more control; you take on hosting, security, testing and updates (module 11)
  • Build: most control and fit; you take on all provider duties and liability
  • Hybrid: a base model plus your data or retrieval; check whether the changes make you a provider (Article 25)
  • Decide with requirements, risk, skills, cost, time and the committee's risk appetite; record the decision
  • Helios: go with conditions: no in-house build until staffing, a quality management system and budget are in place

Exam tip: Choose to build only when the benefits justify the full set of duties that come with it.

5Exam Q&A

5.1 Practice questions (one best answer, or select exactly the number the question asks for)

S1Helios has selected the Corvid Labs model for its customer assistant. The design-stage impact assessment assumed an internal-only tool, but the assistant will now answer customers in public chat. What should the governance lead do?

  • AKeep the design-stage assessment unchanged, because the model and the company are the same as they were at the design stage
  • BWait for the provider to publish its own assessment, and rely on that alone for Helios's use
  • CSkip the assessment, because the provider is responsible for the safety of its own model
  • DUpdate the assessment for the selected system and its public use, with the provider's documents and tests
Show the answer

Answer: D. The deployer assesses its own use of the chosen system. The provider's documents and tests give evidence, but they cannot cover Helios's customers and setting. Public use is a material change, so the assessment must be updated before launch.

S2A company reviews an impact assessment written by the provider of a hiring tool before relying on it. Which TWO checks are most useful? (Select TWO.)

  • AWhether the document carries the provider's logo and a polished professional layout throughout the pages
  • BWhether the document is long enough to mention the full range of AI topics and regulations
  • CWhether it is current for the latest version and covers the company's own use and applicants
  • DWhether it was written by an author who has not seen the tool used in practice
  • EWhether the mitigations have named owners and dates, and the triggers for reassessment are stated
Show the answer

Answer: C, E. A reused assessment must be current and match the deployer's use, and its mitigations need owners, dates and reassessment triggers. Layout, length and an author with no practical knowledge say nothing about quality.

S3A company reviews a vendor's generative AI service agreement. Which term most directly addresses the risk that employees' confidential prompts could be used to train the vendor's model?

  • AA clause limiting the vendor's use of customer data to providing the service, with no training without agreement
  • BA clause that sets the monthly uptime target and the service credits owed to the customer if it is missed
  • CA clause that names the country whose courts will hear disputes between the parties to the agreement
  • DA clause that sets the date on which the first invoice will be issued to the customer by the vendor
Show the answer

Answer: A. Data terms control whether prompts and files may be reused. Uptime, the choice of courts and invoice dates matter to the contract, but none of them stops the vendor training on the customer's inputs.

S4Ravi Menon and Jonas Weber review the Corvid Labs agreement. It lets the vendor replace the model at any time without notice. What is the main risk, and the best fix?

  • AReplacement models are better than the old one, so no change to the terms is needed
  • BThe model's behavior can change after Helios has tested it, so require notice, retest time and version pinning
  • CThe vendor may raise its prices, so the fix is a longer period for paying the vendor's invoices each month
  • DCustomers may notice the change, so the vendor should hide the name of the model it uses from them
Show the answer

Answer: B. A silent model change can invalidate the tests and the impact assessment. The contract should require notice of material changes, time to retest, and the option to stay on a tested version.

S5Which TWO terms in an AI vendor agreement best help the customer meet its own oversight and assessment duties? (Select TWO.)

  • AA clause giving the vendor ownership of everything the customer types into the system and receives from it
  • BAccess to current documentation, such as instructions for use and information about the model
  • CA right for the vendor to show the customer's logo in its own marketing materials and on its website
  • DRights to test or audit the system, and a fixed short notice period for incidents
  • EA statement of the location of the vendor's head office and the size of its global workforce
Show the answer

Answer: B, D. Oversight and assessment need documentation, the right to test or audit, and fast notice of incidents. Ownership of the customer's inputs, logo rights and the vendor's head office do not help the customer meet its duties.

S6A company that uses a vendor's AI system decides to build its own proprietary model for the same purpose. Which statement about its position is correct?

  • AIts obligations stay the same, because the use case is unchanged and the supplier of the model is the one change
  • BIt escapes regulation, because a model used only inside the company is never covered by any law or rule
  • CIt takes on a developer's obligations and higher liability, because no vendor stands between it and the harm
  • DIts liability falls, because it now controls the model and there is no other party to blame for the harm it causes
Show the answer

Answer: C. The company becomes the provider, with the developer's obligations and a greater share of the liability. Building a model does not lower the duties or take the system outside the law.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Assess the chosen system your use, people and data; provider documents plus your own tests; Article 26 and 27 duties; review existing assessments for currency and fit
Vendor terms data use, IP and indemnity, security and incident notice, performance and audit rights, liability, change and exit; know the red flags
Own model you become the provider, with more obligations and higher liability, and also more control and fit
Decide build, buy or both, with eyes open and the decision recorded
